---
title: "Compile your first contract"
description: "Compile a small high-level contract to Charlie locally, inspect its entry points, and understand what deployment adds."
---

Riadchain contracts are written in a small high-level language and compiled to
Charlie, the deterministic language executed by the Rust node. Start with a local
compilation: it needs no wallet, funds or running network.

The CLI below emits Charlie, not an ABI file or a deployment. ABI extraction is
separate source-based tooling. A `constructor` becomes public `init`; deployment
does not call it automatically or enforce one-time initialization.

## Set up the workspace

The compiler currently lives in the private Riadchain repository; source access
is required for this guide. Use Bun with the
repository lockfile; CI currently pins Bun 1.3.11.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/nfl0/riadchain.git
cd riadchain
bun install --frozen-lockfile
```

These examples assume commands run from the repository root. Rust is not needed
to emit Charlie. Native execution tests need the repository's Rust toolchain and
a current native bridge, which is a separate step.

## Write a bounded counter

Save this as `/tmp/riadchain-counter.hl`:

```text
contract Counter {
  storage count: u64
  event CountChanged(indexed sender: address, count: u64)

  view method get() -> u64 {
    let current = storage.count
    if (current == null) { return 0 }
    return current
  }

  method add(by: u64) -> u64 {
    require(by > 0, "positive increment required")
    require(by <= 100, "increment too large")
    let mut current = storage.count
    if (current == null) { current = 0 }
    require(current + by <= 1000000, "counter limit reached")
    storage.count = current + by
    emit CountChanged(ctx.sender, storage.count)
    return storage.count
  }
}
```

Unset storage is `null`, so the example handles the first call explicitly. This
counter deliberately lets every caller increment it. A contract controlling
funds or equipment needs its own authorization rules.

```sh
bun tools/highlevel/compile-file.ts \
  /tmp/riadchain-counter.hl /tmp/riadchain-counter.charlie
```

The command writes Charlie source and prints its byte length. Open the output:
its `main` dispatcher selects `get` or `add` by the `method` field and checks the
typed parameters before invoking the selected method.

For a compiler integration, use the source API:

```ts
import { compileHighLevelContract } from './tools/highlevel/compiler.ts';

const source = await Bun.file('/tmp/riadchain-counter.hl').text();
const code = compileHighLevelContract(source);
console.log(code);
```

## Understand the call data

The `add` method takes named arguments. Its logical input is `{ by: 5n }`, with
`add` supplied as the method selector. For a signed Charlie call, use
[the SDK's typed argument handling](/developers/contract-arguments/). For a
revision 59 read, `client.callView({ contractAddress, method: 'get', args: {} })`
uses the view RPC codec.

Compilation produces code, not a deployed address. The deploy builder needs the
actual deployer, salt, gas limit, live chain identity and funded inputs. Read
[SDK setup](/developers/sdk/) and [transaction flow](/developers/transactions/)
before adding signing or deployment. There is no universal deployed Counter
address in this guide.

## Validate the boundary you changed

A local compiler emission check can run one focused test without executing a
contract or starting a network:

```sh
bun test tests/bun/unit/highlevel-compiler.unit.test.ts \
  --test-name-pattern 'constructor sugar'
```

Compilation alone does not prove execution or host behavior. A contract regression
should also exercise the actual generated code in the current Rust runtime. A
client regression should cover builder → protobuf → native execution, especially
when arguments contain integers. The web IDE offers a local sandbox, with the
[native boundary limitations](/build/charlie-and-native-tokens/) described below.

Source: [compiler and local CLI](https://github.com/nfl0/riadchain/tree/master/tools/highlevel).
